demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: John, a 54-year-old married man and experienced forester, has been struggling with overwhelming distress since an incident on his job three months ago. John accidentally caused serious injury to one of his colleagues during a routine logging operation. He had come to believe that there was something inherently wrong with him, which led to the accident. This belief manifested in an acute sense of guilt and self-doubt, making it increasingly difficult for him to trust himself in any task. The traumatic event unfolded one clear autumn morning when John and his colleague, Alex, were cutting down trees. As they worked together, a sudden gust of wind caused the chain saw to slip from Alex's grasp. The machine swung wildly, slicing into Alex's leg with brutal force. John could still vividly remember the sound of metal tearing through flesh and the immediate shock on Alex's face. Since then, any physical pain in his own body serves as a potent trigger, transporting him back to that horrifying moment. John had been unable to relax even when he knew he was safe at home or in familiar surroundings. The sensation of tension and hypervigilance became a constant companion. His wife noticed this change; John would often sit with an almost rigid posture, his eyes darting around as if expecting something to go wrong at any moment. His occupation as a forester meant that he was regularly exposed to environments where physical proximity and reminders of the accident were inescapable. He began avoiding work sites that resembled the location of the incident, which led to significant delays in completing his projects. His manager had grown increasingly concerned about John's declining performance and frequent absences. John's memories of the event would often resurface unexpectedly, accompanied by intense bodily sensations. When these memories came to mind, he would involuntarily reenact the physical positions and movements from that day. He felt a sense of rage when recalling his own helplessness in preventing Alex's injury. This rage was intertwined with an overwhelming grief for what happened to Alex and the guilt he felt over not being able to prevent it. The belief that he could no longer rely on himself or perform the tasks that had defined him as a forester caused John significant distress. He began avoiding responsibilities at work, fearing that any mistake might lead to another tragedy. This avoidance took its toll; his colleagues noticed his reluctance to engage in critical tasks and the growing distance between them. John's watchfulness over strangers also became pronounced. Even in ordinary situations, he found himself scanning for signs of potential danger or harm. His wife felt a strain on their relationship as well; John often snapped at her if she moved too suddenly or made unexpected noises, which he interpreted as threats. The accumulation of these symptoms and the increasing distance from his work and relationships finally prompted John to seek help. What frightened him most was the idea that he might never regain the confidence and capability that once defined him as a forester. He hoped for a way to reconcile his guilt and regain some semblance of control over his life. John's current state reflects an acute struggle with the belief that there is something inherently wrong with him, which drives his inability to relax and trust himself. His fear of being unable to prevent another tragedy has led to avoidance behaviors and strained relationships. Despite this, John remains hopeful that through therapy, he can find a path forward and reconnect with the person he once was.
